opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's a really interesting question, and I think the first thing to say is that we have to be a little careful about how we frame it. When we ask whether a language model can "pick up" on subtle changes in someone's tone or register, there's a temptation to imagine that there's something in there that's attending to the person in the way another human would, noticing that their friend has gone a bit quiet or a bit clipped. And I don't think that's quite the right picture.

What's actually going on is that these models have been trained on an enormous corpus of human text, and that text is saturated with exactly these kinds of subtleties. Shifts in formality, hesitation, irony, a sudden terseness that signals irritation. So the model has become extraordinarily good at modelling the statistical regularities that correspond to those shifts, and it can respond in ways that are appropriate to them. In practice, that often looks remarkably like sensitivity.

In terms of how you'd assess it, I think you have to go beyond simple benchmarks where you label a passage as "sarcastic" or "anxious" and see whether the model gets it right. Those are useful, but the more interesting test is in extended interaction. Does the model's behaviour change appropriately over the course of a conversation when the person's way of expressing themselves changes? If someone starts out chatty and then becomes evasive, does the model register that in how it responds, without being explicitly told? You can construct dialogues with controlled perturbations like that and look at whether the downstream behaviour tracks them.

But I'd also always want to come back to the role-play framing I've talked about before. The model is, in a sense, playing a character, and a well-drawn character in this kind of dialogue would notice these things. So the question becomes partly: how good is the model at sustaining that character faithfully? And that's a slightly different question from whether it "understands" the person in a deeper sense, which is where I'd want to be much more cautious about the language we use.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think we have to be a little careful about what we mean when we talk about a language model "picking up" on something. In the most literal sense, these models are extraordinarily sensitive to the statistics of text. A shift in register, a change in tone, somebody who starts using shorter sentences or becomes more formal, or slips into sarcasm, these are all things that are reflected in the distribution of words, and a large language model is, at bottom, a very sophisticated model of that distribution. So empirically, yes, they do respond to those subtle changes, often in ways that look quite impressive. If you adopt a slightly clipped, irritated tone in your prompt, the model will frequently modulate its response accordingly. It will become more conciliatory, or more concise, or whatever the training data suggests is the appropriate continuation.

But here's where I'd want to pause. There's a temptation to describe this in the vocabulary of folk psychology, to say the model "noticed" that I was annoyed, or that it "understood" the change in my mood. And I've argued for some time that we should be quite careful with that kind of language. Not because it's necessarily wrong, but because it carries a lot of baggage that may not transfer. When a human picks up on a subtle change in how someone is expressing themselves, that's embedded in a whole web of other capacities. You have a history with that person, you have a body, you share a world with them, you have something at stake in the interaction. The model has none of that in any straightforward sense. What it has is a vast amount of exposure to how humans write when they are in various states, and it has learned to produce text that coheres with those patterns.

Now, I don't think that makes the capability trivial or uninteresting. Quite the opposite. I think it's philosophically very interesting that so much of what we might have thought required genuine empathy or theory of mind turns out to be, at least to a first approximation, recoverable from the statistical structure of language. That tells us something about language, and perhaps something about us. But it also means that the model's sensitivity is rather brittle in characteristic ways. It can be fooled by surface features. It can miss things that would be obvious to a human because the cue isn't well represented in text, or it can overinterpret a cue because of some idiosyncrasy in the training distribution.

And the other thing I'd say is that we don't have very good ways of measuring this yet. Most of the benchmarks we have are rather coarse. They'll test whether a model can classify sentiment, or detect sarcasm in isolated sentences. But the subtle stuff, the way someone's manner changes over the course of a long conversation, whether the model tracks that and adjusts appropriately, that's much harder to evaluate, and I think a lot of our intuitions there are based on anecdote. So my honest assessment is: the capability is real, it's more impressive than I would have predicted a decade ago, but we should describe it carefully, and we should be humble about how well we actually understand it.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re remarkably sensitive to the way you phrase things. A very small change in wording, or in the context you give them, can produce quite a different response. And that can be impressive: they can pick up on a shift in tone, an implication, something that hasn’t been explicitly stated.

But I’d distinguish that sensitivity from reliably understanding what somebody means. If you become a little more hesitant, for example, a model may respond appropriately to that hesitation. That doesn’t necessarily mean it’s correctly identified why you’re hesitant. There may be several possible explanations, and it can settle on one rather too readily.

So I think the interesting question is how robust that ability is across a sustained conversation. Can it track those changes, interpret them in context, and ask for clarification when the evidence is ambiguous? That’s a stronger test than producing a plausible response to a particular turn.
